extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and computational number theorists working on Mochizuki's IUT, elliptic curves, and explicit anabelian/arithmetic-geometry constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and implement the definition of Mochizuki's "initial theta data" for an elliptic curve over Q (or a number field), listing the algebraic/Galois/torsion/placewise conditions and providing algorithmic checks and constructions. Includes explicit worked example (E11a1) and pseudocode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-arithmetic (pre-theta)
rubrics_metrics.description: EC \ o is not an arithmetic Riemann surface (where o is the identity of the elliptic curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excludes CM curves and the finite list of Sijsling j-invariants; see Theorem 2.3.6 and Remark 2.4.2. Practical test: check j_E ∉ {0,1728,214313/53,22733/34} (is_sijsling()). The paper explains equivalences of arithmeticity (Shimura/Margulis) and gives examples (e.g. E11a1 is non-arithmetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-isotrivial / large mod-ℓ image (pre-theta)
rubrics_metrics.description: F/Q(j_E) is Galois and the mod-ℓ Galois representation ρ_ℓ(G_F) ⊂ Aut(E[ℓ](F)) contains a subgroup isomorphic to SL2(𝔽_ℓ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition precludes geometric CM (Galois image abelian). In practice one asks for ρ_ℓ to be surjective or to contain SL2; can be checked using OpenImage implementations (Zywina/Rouse–Sutherland–Zureick-Brown) or Magma. See §2.4(2), §2.10.7, and algorithmic discussion in §2.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torsion conditions (pre-theta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field F must contain −1 and E(F) must contain the indicated torsion (the paper imposes E(F) ⊃ E(F)[30] in place of Mochizuki's original 6-torsion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: Mochizuki's original uses 6-torsion but later material requires 30-torsion so the authors impose E(F)[30]. Mazur's theorem limits rational torsion over Q; computing these torsion points can be done via Tate/uniformization locally and mapped to Q-points (see §2.10.5). Numerical vs theoretical caveats noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Places of multiplicative reduction S (pre-theta)
rubrics_metrics.description: S ⊂ V(Q(j_E))_0 is a non-empty set of finite places such that every v ∈ S has odd residue characteristic and every model E_{Q(j_E)} of E over Q(j_E) has multiplicative reduction at v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S must be non-empty; in examples S = {11} for E11a1. The Tate parameter q_v and its valuation ord_v(q_v) play a role in later congruence constraints. See §2.4(4) and §2.10.2–2.10.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence conditions on ℓ and S (pre-theta)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the chosen prime ℓ and for all v ∈ S require: (a) ℓ ∤ char(v); (b) ℓ ∤ ord_v(q_v); (c) ℓ ≥ 5; (d) ℓ ∤ [F : Q(j_E)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modular/congruence constraints ensure the local Tate-uniformization arguments and global Galois/representation hypotheses work. (b) uses the valuation of the Tate parameter at places of multiplicative reduction. See Definition 2.4.1(5) and examples in §2.10.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local multiplicative subspace and local canonical generator (Tate-uniformization)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a p-adic local field L with E/L having multiplicative reduction and a prime ℓ≥3 with ℓ ∤ ord_L(j_E), there is a canonical inclusion μ_ℓ(L) ↪ E(L)[ℓ] (the local multiplicative subspace) and a canonical generator of the quotient given by the class of q^{1/ℓ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 2.7.2 (existence of a transvection/unipotent element in the mod-ℓ representation) and the Tate uniformization (ϕ : L^×/q^ℤ → E(L)) give explicit P1 = ϕ(ζ_ℓ) and P2 = ϕ(q^{1/ℓ}). The local canonical generator is the image of q^{1/ℓ} modulo ⟨ζ_ℓ,q⟩; ord_L(q)=ord_L(Δ_E) ties this to discriminant. See §2.5–2.7 and (2.1)–(2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of global multiplicative subspace M
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgroup M ⊂ E[ℓ](K) (K = F(E[ℓ])) is a global multiplicative subspace for a place w (or for a set S of places) if, after viewing M in Ev(K_w), one has M_w = μ_ℓ(w) as a G(w/v)-module for each w lying over v in the chosen lift V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Globalizing the local μ_ℓ(w) everywhere is impossible in general; instead one 'rigs' V (a choice of lifts V ⊂ V(K)) so that for each chosen w ∈ V one attains M_w = μ_ℓ(w). Lemma 2.9.2 gives a construction using G_F-transitivity and choice of σ_v. See §2.7–2.9; the paper stresses this is a 'fake' global multiplicative subspace obtained by choosing V appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global canonical generator ϵ (spin canonical generator)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element ϵ ∈ M is a (spin) global canonical generator for S if for each w ∈ S the image of ϵ_w in M_w (≅ Z/ℓ) equals ± the local canonical generator at w.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ϵ is only significant up to ±1. In Mochizuki's original formulation this corresponds to a cusp of an auxiliary orbicurve C_K; the equivalence of formulations is discussed in Remark 2.9.3(2). See Definitions 2.7.3, 2.7.5, and 2.8.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fricke involution / Fricke compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The subgroup M appearing in the theta data must be compatible with the Fricke involution: M should match the Fricke involute corresponding to the chosen cyclic subgroup in the Y_0(ℓ) moduli problem (equivalently, M corresponds to the kernel of the associated Fricke isogeny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 2.2.1 describes the Fricke involution (E,M) ↦ (E/M, E[ℓ]/M) and the associated Fricke isogeny f : E → E/M. In Definition 2.8.1 the authors require M to be the Fricke involute of the chosen subgroup; this ties the global multiplicative subspace to the Y_0(ℓ)-data. See §2.2 and §2.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full initial theta data tuple requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial theta data is the tuple (F, ℓ, E, S, V, M, ϵ) where (F, ℓ, E, S) is pre-theta data (satisfying the numbered pre-theta conditions) and (V, M, ϵ) realize a (fake) global multiplicative subspace and a global canonical generator with respect to the chosen lift V of places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 2.8.1 collects the above pieces: M must be the Fricke involute and a global multiplicative subspace for V ∩ V(K)_S and ϵ ∈ M(F) must be a global canonical generator for that set. The paper emphasizes bookkeeping and the two-chunk breakdown (pre-theta data and the (V,M,ϵ) simulation). See §2.4 and §2.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible prime ℓ selection (algorithmic criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a small prime ℓ with the following properties: ℓ ≥ 5; ℓ ∤ conductor N(E); for every bad prime p in the conductor, ℓ ∤ ord_p(q_p) (Tate parameter valuation); ℓ ∤ [F : Q(j_E)]; and the mod-ℓ representation over the working field F (often F = Q(i,E[30])) is surjective (or contains SL2). Also require linear disjointness conditions (e.g. Q(E[ℓ]) ∩ Q(E[60]) = Q) to ensure surjectivity over F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm 1 and 2 implement these checks (get_l, get_theta_data). The paper discusses using OpenImage (Zywina/RSZB) and Galois-group counts to test linear disjointness (|G_{ab}| = |G_a|·|G_b|). Example: ℓ = 13 works for E11a1. Practical caveat: computing full torsion fields may be expensive; OpenImage gives a way to read off ℓ which do not divide the computed M in GL_2(ℤ/Mℤ). See §2.10.6, §2.11 and Algorithm 1/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity / large image testing and linear disjointness
rubrics_metrics.description: To guarantee the representation ρ_ℓ over the chosen field F is large (surjective), require either direct surjectivity checks (ρ_{ℓ,F} surjective) or verify two conditions: ρ_{ℓ,ℚ} is surjective and Q(E[ℓ]) is linearly disjoint from the auxiliary field (e.g. Q(E[60]) containing Q(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OpenImage algorithm (Rouse–Sutherland–Zureick-Brown, Zywina implementations) to compute images and deduce for which ℓ the mod-ℓ representation is surjective. Linear disjointness is tested via Galois group product formula (|G_{ab}| = |G_a|·|G_b|). See the discussion in §2.11 and Theorem 2.11.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computability and algorithmic caveats for initial theta data
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the construction and checks are Turing computable (there is pseudo-code in §2.11), computing initial theta data in practice often requires splitting/torsion fields (e.g. 30-torsion field) and large Galois computations that are impractical for many curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors provide Sage-style pseudocode (Algorithm 1 & 2) and point to computational tools (Sage, Magma, OpenImage repository). Line 12 in Algorithm 2 asks to compute the 30-torsion field; get_global_multiplicative_subspace() relies on that splitting field. The paper remarks these are computable but not practical for large instances and cites implementations and references (Zywina, RSZB, Magma forks). See §2.11 and remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude Sijsling j-invariants (practical non-arithmetic test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically test non-arithmeticity by verifying j_E is not one of the finite Sijsling invariants j_E ∈ {0, 1728, 214313/53, 22733/34}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper provides is_sijsling() as a helper function used in Algorithm 2; this is a necessary preliminary admissibility filter. See Theorem 2.3.6 and Algorithm 2 (line: if is_sijsling(j0) then return False).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tate parameter valuation relation and use
rubrics_metrics.description: At a place of multiplicative reduction the Tate parameter q satisfies ord_L(q)=ord_L(Δ_{E}), and congruence conditions require ℓ ∤ ord_v(q_v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties the local uniformization/Tate-curve computations to the congruence conditions (Definition 2.4.1(5b)). The paper shows how to compute q_v p-adically (examples for p=11 are given to many 11-adic digits) and uses these valuations in get_l and Algorithm 1 checks. See §2.5 and §2.10.4–2.10.6.
